extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, biogeographers, and evolutionary biologists (general scientific readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and empirical patterns that a satisfactory explanation of geographical distribution (especially island biogeography) should account for; includes dispersal, endemism, barriers, historical change, and organismal interactions. Suitable for assessing theories of colonisation, creation, or descent with modification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scarcity of kinds on oceanic islands
rubrics_metrics.description: The species of all kinds which inhabit oceanic islands are few in number compared with those on equal continental areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin cites comparisons (New Zealand: 750 flowering plants vs. similar continental areas; Cambridge county: 847, Anglesea: 764) and examples like Ascension and St. Helena. He argues that this scarcity cannot be fully explained by physical conditions alone; any satisfactory theory must explain why oceanic islands have fewer native kinds despite some islands' large area and variety of stations. Under the creation view this would require admitting fewer creations on islands; under migration/modification it follows from rarity of successful colonisation and subsequent naturalisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: High proportion of endemic species on islands
rubrics_metrics.description: Although kinds are few, the proportion of endemic species (those found nowhere else) on islands is often extremely large.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: endemic land-shells of Madeira, endemic birds of the Galapagos. Darwin explains this by occasional arrivals followed by modification (natural selection) in isolation. A theory must account for why islands often host many peculiar species in particular classes or sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differential endemism depending on dispersal facility
rubrics_metrics.description: Different classes or sections of organisms on the same island may show different degrees of endemism depending on their facility of immigration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin notes that nearly every land-bird in the Galapagos is peculiar but only two of eleven marine birds are; Bermuda and Madeira have few or no endemic land-birds because many continental birds visit them. Sea-shells are often not endemic because their larvae or eggs can be transported by seaweed, driftwood, or birds, whereas land-shells are more often endemic. Any theory must explain taxon-specific patterns via dispersal ability and immigration history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ecological replacement of absent groups
rubrics_metrics.description: When certain classes are absent on islands, other groups often occupy their ecological places (e.g., reptiles or giant wingless birds taking the place of mammals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin gives Galapagos reptiles and New Zealand wingless birds as examples. He argues that such patterns are not necessarily due to physical conditions but often to differential facility of immigration and subsequent modification; a good explanation must account for functionally equivalent replacements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insular modification of growth-form (herbaceous to arboreal)
rubrics_metrics.description: On islands, herbaceous orders sometimes give rise to bushes and ultimately trees, producing trees belonging to orders otherwise herbaceous elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin reasons that trees have confined ranges and are unlikely to reach remote islands; where trees are absent, herbaceous plants can gain advantage by growing taller, so natural selection favors increased stature. A satisfactory theory should explain island floras having trees from ordinarily herbaceous lineages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of batrachians from oceanic islands due to transport intolerance
rubrics_metrics.description: Frogs, toads, and newts (batrachians) have never been found on many oceanic islands; their eggs and spawn are immediately killed by sea-water, making cross-sea transport unlikely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin verified Bory St. Vincent’s assertion and cites introductions (Madeira, Azores, Mauritius) where humans introduced frogs which then multiplied. Any theory must explain the general absence of batrachians by reference to dispersal barriers, not physical unfitness of island environments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of terrestrial mammals vs presence of aerial mammals (bats)
rubrics_metrics.description: Terrestrial mammals are generally absent from isolated oceanic islands beyond a certain distance, whereas aerial mammals (bats) are often present and even endemic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin reports no clear instance of wild terrestrial mammals inhabiting islands >300 miles from a continent, while many islands possess endemic bats. He argues bats can reach islands by flight and then be modified in isolation. The criterion: theories must account for presence/absence patterns by dispersal capacities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sea-depth between island and mainland correlates with faunal affinity
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a relation between the depth of the sea separating an island from the mainland and the similarity or affinity of the mammalian fauna (or allied species) between them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Malay Archipelago (deep channel separating distinct faunas), Britain/Europe (shallow channel, same mammals), West Indian Islands on a deep submerged bank have distinct American forms. Darwin links depth to likelihood of past land connection and to the degree of subsequent modification; a good theory must incorporate bathymetry and past geographic change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affinity of island biotas to the nearest mainland
rubrics_metrics.description: Endemic productions of islands are generally related to those of the nearest continent (or other nearby islands); e.g., Galapagos biota resemble South America, Cape de Verde resemble Africa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin highlights the Galapagos as 'bearing the unmistakeable stamp of the American continent' despite dissimilar physical conditions. He argues this is inexplicable by independent creation but follows from colonisation from the nearest source and subsequent modification. Any explanatory framework must predict this nearest-source affinity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Within-archipelago close affinity with inter-island endemism
rubrics_metrics.description: Islands within the same archipelago tend to be tenanted by very closely related but distinct species; inhabitants of each separate island are more closely related to each other than to species elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Galapagos islands show marvellous close relations but substantial inter-island distinctness. Darwin explains this by occasional colonisation patterns (same original sources or stepping-stone colonisation), differing biotic communities producing different selective regimes, and imperfect inter-island dispersal; a theory must explain both close affinity and island-specific differentiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of universal spread of newly formed species due to isolation and pre-occupation
rubrics_metrics.description: New species formed on one island (or area) do not necessarily spread quickly to neighbouring islands even if they are capable of dispersal; pre-occupation by well-adapted resident species and effective isolation often prevent spread.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin uses examples: three distinct mocking-thrush species each confined to their own Galapagos island; Porto Santo and Madeira land-shells (despite stone transport) remain distinct. He notes that naturalised species that spread rapidly often are not closely allied to natives and thus have competitive advantages. A valid theory must incorporate competitive exclusion and the role of pre-occupation in limiting range expansion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation between dispersal ability, variability, and wide geographic range
rubrics_metrics.description: Genera or species capable of wide dispersal often include species with very wide ranges; widely-ranging species tend to vary and give rise to new forms, which determines average range within genera.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin cites world-ranging bird genera, bats, Felidae, Canidae, butterflies, beetles, and freshwater organisms. He emphasizes that wide range requires both crossing barriers and ability to compete successfully in new lands; a satisfactory model of distribution must connect dispersal capacity with propensity to vary and speciate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lower/slowly-changing organisms tend to range more widely
rubrics_metrics.description: Organisms low in the scale of life, which generally change more slowly, often range more widely and retain the same specific character; minute seeds/eggs aid distant transport.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin refers to the law discussed by Alph. de Candolle: the lower any group of organisms is, the more widely it is apt to range. Geological antiquity and slow change also allow more time for diffusion. The criterion: distribution explanations must account for taxonomic rank/rate-of-change effects on range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of barriers, biotic interactions, and historical/geological change
rubrics_metrics.description: Barriers (land or water) and the mutual relations of organisms are of the highest importance in determining distribution; past climatic changes (e.g., glacial periods) and changes in land levels must be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin asserts these principles explain localisation of sub-genera, genera, families, and why areas with similar physical conditions may harbour different biotas. Explanations must integrate biotic interactions, barriers, and historical events (glaciation, changes of level) to be satisfactory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity of ranges in time and space with explainable exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally the area inhabited by a species or group is continuous in space and time; exceptions (discontinuous occurrences) should be explainable by past migration under different conditions or extinction in intermediate tracts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin treats discontinuities as usually attributable to migration at former periods, occasional transport, or local extinctions; a credible theory must not treat such exceptions as inexplicable anomalies but account for historical processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of submerged/vanished 'halting-places' and need to investigate transport mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: The probability that now-submerged islands or former halting-places aided colonisation should not be overlooked; our ignorance of many curious means of occasional transport requires experimental investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin gives land-shell flotation and survival experiments as an example and argues more experiments are needed on means of dispersal (e.g., drifted timber, adhesion to birds). A comprehensive theory must allow for episodic and poorly-understood transport events and encourage empirical testing of dispersal mechanisms.
